name: Answer Types
description: Classify answers as defense, indict, turn, or offense, and choose the kind a round needs.

lesson.title: Know what your answer does
lesson.summary: Tell defense, indicts, turns, and offense apart by what each accomplishes, and pick what the round needs.

content.objective: Classify answers by what they do — defense, indict, turn, or offense — and choose the kind of answer the round actually needs.
content.explanation: Suppose the other side argues that a new downtown park will hurt nearby shops. You could answer in several ways, and each answer DOES a different job. If you show the harm is smaller or shakier than claimed, that is a defensive answer: when it succeeds, their argument gets smaller or less credible, but nothing new counts for you. One special kind of defense is the INDICT: you attack the argument's support — the source, the reasoning, the assumptions behind it — so the judge trusts it less. An indict weakens; it never reverses. An OFFENSIVE answer does a different job: it creates a reason the judge should prefer YOUR side. A simple way to keep them straight: defense explains why they lose an argument; offense creates a reason you win. The most surprising offensive move is the TURN, a reversal: followed honestly, the argument they made becomes a reason for your side — the harm they warned about points the other way, or the measure they chose favours you. These are functional categories, not magic labels: what matters is what the answer accomplishes if it succeeds, not what you call it. The refutation structure — they say, but, because, therefore — still tells you HOW to state any answer; this lesson is about WHAT KIND of answer you are making inside that structure. Turns also come in named varieties you will meet in a later lesson; for now, the skill is spotting the reversal.
content.whyMatters: Judges vote for reasons, not for damage. Defense is not bad — a clean defensive answer is often exactly what a moment needs — and depending on what each side must prove and what remains standing, defense can sometimes be enough. The strategic risk comes when some of their offense survives and you have built no offense of your own: you may have made their case smaller all round without giving the judge a competing reason to prefer your side.
steps: Restate what they claimed, in one sentence.
Name the part your response attacks: the claim itself, its support, or where it leads.
Ask: if this response fully succeeds, what is now true in the round?
Decide the direction: did their argument only get weaker or smaller, or does something now count for your side?
Classify: weaker only is defense (an indict if you attacked its support); counting for you is offense (a turn if their own argument was reversed to help you).

workedExample.prompt: Topic: the city should turn a downtown parking lot into a public park. Opponent: shoppers will lose parking, so nearby businesses will lose customers. Response A: their claim rests on a survey of what business owners fear, not on any sales data. Response B: in similar projects, the park brought shops more foot traffic than the parking spots ever did — their business concern favours the park. Classify each response.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Both responses beat the business argument, so both count as offense for our side.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Response A is an indict: if it succeeds, the judge trusts their support less and the argument weakens — but they only lose ground; nothing counts for us yet. Response B is a turn: if it succeeds, the business concern they raised now argues FOR the park, so the judge gains a reason to prefer our side. In the refutation structure both begin the same way — they say shoppers are lost, but... — the difference is what each answer accomplishes.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer classifies by outcome — what is true if the response succeeds — instead of by how forceful the response sounds. Weakening the support is an indict; making their own concern point your way is a turn.

guidedQuestion.prompt: The opponent argues your school recycling plan is too expensive. You answer: the plan is fully paid for by an existing county grant, so no school money is spent. Your answer completely succeeds. What kind of answer was it?
choices: Defense — the cost objection is gone, but the judge still has no new reason to support recycling
Offense — any answer that fully succeeds becomes offense
A turn — the cost argument now helps your side
An indict — you attacked the source of their cost figures
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Defense — the cost objection is gone, but the judge still has no new reason to support recycling
guidedQuestion.hint: Ask what is true after the answer succeeds — did anything start counting FOR you?
guidedQuestion.explanation: This is the classic trap: a strong, completely successful answer can still be pure defense. Success is not what makes offense — direction is. The cost argument is removed, which is real progress, but removal only means they lose that argument; nothing here gives the judge a reason to vote for recycling. And no source was attacked, so it is not an indict.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Topic: ban single-use plastic bags. Opponent: reusable cotton bags are worse for the environment, because making one takes far more resources than making one plastic bag. You answer: one reusable bag replaces hundreds of plastic ones over its life, so on the environmental measure they chose, the ban comes out ahead. What did your answer do?
choices: Played defense — it only shows their resource number is smaller than claimed
Indicted their evidence — it attacks where their resource figures came from
Turned the argument — the environmental concern they raised now counts in favour of the ban
Changed the subject to a different advantage of the ban
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Turned the argument — the environmental concern they raised now counts in favour of the ban
practiceQuestions.hint: Follow their own measure to its honest conclusion — whose side does it land on?
practiceQuestions.explanation: This is a reversal. You accepted their measure — total environmental cost — and showed that, counted over whole lifetimes, it favours the ban. Their concern became your reason, and that reversal is exactly what makes a turn. Merely shrinking their number would have been defense, and nothing here questions their sources, so it is not an indict.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Opponent: the new stadium will boost the local economy, according to a report. You answer: that report was commissioned by the stadium's own developer and counts spending that would have happened in town anyway. If your answer succeeds, what has it accomplished?
choices: A turn — attacking their evidence flips the economy argument to your side
An indict — the judge trusts the report less, so the economy argument carries less weight, but it does not count for your side
Offense — it gives the judge a new reason of your own to oppose the stadium
It proves stadiums harm local economies everywhere
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: An indict — the judge trusts the report less, so the economy argument carries less weight, but it does not count for your side
practiceQuestions.hint: Weakening their support and reversing their argument are different jobs.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Indict and turn are not the same move. An indict attacks the argument's support — here the report's incentives and its counting method — so the argument weakens. A turn would require the economy issue to end up favouring your side, and nothing here does that. Even a devastating indict is still defense: their loss, not your gain.

practiceQuestions.prompt: They claim school uniforms reduce bullying, citing a small survey. You read a much larger, better-designed study finding uniforms have no effect on bullying. A teammate whispers: great, that turns their argument. Is the teammate right?
choices: Yes — whenever your evidence is better than theirs, the argument is turned
Yes — a larger study always converts an argument into offense
No — because surveys can never be answered with studies
No — stronger counter-evidence is still defense here, because a finding of no effect cancels their advantage without making bullying a reason for your side
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: No — stronger counter-evidence is still defense here, because a finding of no effect cancels their advantage without making bullying a reason for your side
practiceQuestions.hint: A turn needs a reversal. Did the bullying issue end up pointing at your side?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Better evidence makes an answer stronger, not offensive. A finding of no effect neutralises their advantage — excellent defense — but the bullying issue now counts for nobody. If your study had instead found uniforms increase bullying, the issue would point your way and you would have a turn. What the answer accomplishes, not the quality of the evidence, decides the label.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Your rebuttal answered all three of their arguments with clean defensive answers and one sharp indict, and you spent no time on your own case. Their strongest argument survives in weakened form. What is the strategic gap?
choices: Defensive answers were the wrong choice — every answer should have been a turn
You made their case smaller but never gave the judge anything that counts for your side, so their surviving argument can still decide the round
Indicts should never be used while any opposing argument survives
There is no gap — weakening all three arguments guarantees the win
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: You made their case smaller but never gave the judge anything that counts for your side, so their surviving argument can still decide the round
practiceQuestions.hint: After all that defense, what reason does the judge have to vote FOR you?
practiceQuestions.explanation: None of the defensive answers was a mistake — defense is often exactly the right tool, and here it did real work. The gap is what you relied on it to accomplish: defense can only shrink what they have, never build what you need. With part of their offense standing and yours unextended, the judge's only surviving reason belongs to them. The round needed at least one source of offense — your extended case, a turn, or both.

masteryCheck.prompt: The opponent argues that keeping the library open later will exhaust its staff. Which response is a TURN?
choices: The plan funds two new part-time hires, so nobody's shift gets longer
Their exhaustion claim comes from a staffing report about a far larger city system
Evening shifts are the shifts our staff most often request, so on their own staff-wellbeing concern, the later hours are an improvement
Later hours also let working parents visit, which is a separate benefit
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Evening shifts are the shifts our staff most often request, so on their own staff-wellbeing concern, the later hours are an improvement
masteryCheck.hint: Three of these help you. Only one makes THEIR concern argue for your side.
masteryCheck.explanation: Walk the labels. The part-time hires answer removes the harm — defense. The larger-city report answer attacks their support — an indict, which is still defense. Working parents is offense, but it is a new independent reason, not a reversal. Only the shift-request answer takes the very concern they raised — staff wellbeing — and shows it favours later hours: their argument now helps you, which is what a turn is.

masteryCheck.prompt: Final speech, four minutes left. Their case is mostly answered, but one of their advantages survives your defense, and your own case has not been mentioned since your first speech. What does this round need most?
choices: More defensive answers piled onto the surviving advantage, since defense got you this far
A restatement that their other arguments were all answered
New indicts against evidence the judge has already discounted
Something the judge can vote for: extend your own offense or a turn, and weigh it against their surviving advantage
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Something the judge can vote for: extend your own offense or a turn, and weigh it against their surviving advantage
masteryCheck.hint: Decide what the judge is missing, then pick the answer type that supplies it.
masteryCheck.explanation: The classification model also works in reverse: instead of labelling an answer, ask what the round is missing. The judge currently holds one live reason — theirs. More defense might shave it further but cannot hand the judge a reason to choose you; that job belongs to offense. Extending your case or a turn, then weighing it against what survives, supplies the missing piece. Defense got you here and was the right call earlier — it is simply the wrong tool for this last job.

name: Case Topic and Definitions
description: Turn a resolution into a fair, debatable case.

lesson.title: Set a fair case topic
lesson.summary: Learn resolution, case topic, definitions, and contentions.

content.objective: Create a case topic with clear definitions and contentions.
content.explanation: A resolution is the broad prompt. A case topic is the specific debate you create from it. Definitions explain key terms, and contentions are the main reasons the case should win.
content.whyMatters: A fair case topic invites clash. If it is too vague, too narrow, or dependent on hidden knowledge, the round becomes less educational.
steps: Start from the resolution.
Choose a clear case topic.
Define key terms fairly.
Write distinct contentions.

workedExample.prompt: Resolution: This House values education reform.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Education should be better.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Case topic: public high schools should require a financial literacy course. Definitions: require means graduation requirement. Contentions: student debt prevention and practical career readiness.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer turns a broad resolution into a specific, debatable case.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What is a case topic?
choices: The specific issue debated from a resolution
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: The specific issue debated from a resolution
guidedQuestion.hint: It narrows the broad prompt.
guidedQuestion.explanation: A case topic is the actual issue the round will debate.

practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To set fair boundaries
practiceQuestions.hint: Definitions shape the debate.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Clear definitions help both sides understand what is being debated.

choices: A main reason for the case
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A main reason for the case
practiceQuestions.hint: Contentions support the case.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Contentions are the major arguments for the proposal.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What makes a fair case topic?
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: It creates clear clash
practiceQuestions.hint: Fair topics can be debated by both sides.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A fair case gives both sides a meaningful path to argue.

masteryCheck.prompt: A case topic is so narrow that opposition has no answer. What is the issue?
masteryCheck.explanation: A case should be specific but still debatable.

name: Claim, Warrant, Impact
description: Turn an idea into a complete argument the judge can evaluate.

lesson.title: Build a complete argument
lesson.summary: Learn the claim-warrant-impact pattern for stronger speeches.

content.objective: Write an argument with a clear claim, warrant, and impact.
content.explanation: A complete argument has three parts: the claim says what you believe, the warrant explains why it is true, and the impact explains why it matters in the round.
content.whyMatters: Judges cannot give full credit to an idea they cannot follow. This pattern makes your reasoning visible and gives later speeches something to extend.
steps: Name the claim in one direct sentence.
Add a warrant that explains the cause or logic.
End with the impact: who is affected, how much, and why it matters more than the other side.

workedExample.prompt: Schools should teach practical AI literacy.
workedExample.weakAnswer: AI literacy is important because AI is everywhere.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Schools should teach practical AI literacy because students already use AI tools for research and writing. If they learn limits, bias checks, and responsible use, they make fewer mistakes and are better prepared for college and work.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer states a claim, explains the mechanism, and gives a concrete impact.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which sentence is the warrant?
choices: Schools should teach practical AI literacy.
Students already use AI tools for research and writing.
Prepared students make fewer mistakes in college and work.
This debate is about education policy.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Students already use AI tools for research and writing.
guidedQuestion.hint: The warrant is the reason the claim is true.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This sentence explains why AI literacy belongs in school: students are already using the tools.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which answer has all three parts?
choices: We affirm because the plan is good.
The plan improves safety because trained students can identify AI errors before relying on them, which reduces academic and workplace harm.
The negative side has no evidence.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The plan improves safety because trained students can identify AI errors before relying on them, which reduces academic and workplace harm.
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for claim, reason, and why it matters.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This choice includes the position, the mechanism, and the impact.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should come after a claim?
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A warrant
practiceQuestions.hint: The next step is explaining why the claim is true.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A warrant connects the claim to logic or evidence.

practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The reason a point matters
practiceQuestions.hint: Ask: why should the judge care?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The impact explains the importance or consequence of the argument.

masteryCheck.prompt: A judge asks why your argument matters. Which part are they asking for?
masteryCheck.hint: The word matters points to the consequence.
masteryCheck.explanation: Impact tells the judge why the argument should affect the decision.

name: Clash
description: Find the real disagreement and answer it directly.

lesson.title: Create direct clash
lesson.summary: Learn how to identify and resolve the main disagreement.

content.objective: Identify what both sides disagree about and answer that point directly.
content.explanation: Clash happens when two arguments meet on the same point. It starts with finding what the two sides actually disagree about — not what they both accept. A responsive answer targets the opponent's reasoning on that disputed point: repeating your own case is not clash, and answering a claim the opponent never made is not clash either. The strongest clash goes one step further and explains why your direct answer changes the disputed issue in your favour.
content.whyMatters: Rounds are won on comparison. Clash shows the judge that you are not just speaking well, you are winning the debate.
steps: Name the opponent's claim.
State your answer.
Explain why your answer matters more or proves their claim wrong.

workedExample.prompt: Opponent says the plan costs too much.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Our plan is still good.
workedExample.strongAnswer: On cost, they assume a new class is required. Our plan uses existing advisory time, so their budget objection does not apply.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer names the opposing argument and directly removes its assumption.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which response creates clash?
choices: On cost, their objection assumes a new class, but our plan uses advisory time.
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: On cost, their objection assumes a new class, but our plan uses advisory time.
guidedQuestion.hint: Look for a direct answer to the other side.
guidedQuestion.explanation: This response meets the cost argument directly.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Side A argues a longer lunch break improves focus in afternoon classes. Side B argues the schedule cannot fit a longer lunch without cutting class time. Where is the real disagreement?
choices: Whether the schedule can absorb a longer lunch, since Side B never disputed the focus benefit
Whether focus matters in afternoon classes
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Whether the schedule can absorb a longer lunch, since Side B never disputed the focus benefit
practiceQuestions.hint: Find the point Side B actually contests.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Side B accepts the focus claim and attacks the schedule fit, so that is where the clash lives. Engaging anything else answers a point nobody disputed.

choices: They say cost, we answer with existing time.
They say safety, we answer with training.
Our first contention is still true.
They say delay, we answer with phase-in.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Our first contention is still true.
practiceQuestions.hint: Repeating your case is not direct clash.
practiceQuestions.explanation: This does not answer a specific opposing argument.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The opponent argues a school garden takes up field space used for sports. Which reply creates clash?
choices: Gardens teach responsibility, which is our first contention.
The garden plan uses the unused corner lot, so no field space is lost.
Sports are also valuable to students.
We will now summarise our own case.
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The garden plan uses the unused corner lot, so no field space is lost.
practiceQuestions.hint: Which reply meets the space objection itself?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Only the corner-lot answer engages the opponent's actual objection. Restating your contention or agreeing sports matter leaves the space argument standing.

masteryCheck.prompt: If the opponent says your plan is unrealistic, what should you answer first?
masteryCheck.explanation: Directly answering feasibility creates clash.

name: Constructive Speeches
description: Build the first version of your case clearly and strategically.

lesson.title: Build a constructive speech
lesson.summary: Learn what belongs in the first major speech.

content.objective: Write a constructive speech with definitions, contentions, and impacts.
content.explanation: A constructive speech builds the foundation of the round. It should define the topic, present major contentions, and explain impacts.
content.whyMatters: Later speeches depend on this foundation. If the constructive is vague, rebuttals become harder and the judge has less to evaluate.
steps: Define key terms.
Present two or three contentions.
Explain the warrant and impact for each contention.

workedExample.prompt: Opening government speech on AI literacy.
workedExample.weakAnswer: AI literacy is good and students need it.
workedExample.strongAnswer: We define AI literacy as practical training in responsible tool use. Contention one: it improves academic integrity because students learn limits and citation habits. Contention two: it improves career readiness because students practice safe workplace use.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer defines terms and creates organized contentions.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What belongs in a constructive speech?
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Definitions and contentions
guidedQuestion.hint: Constructives build the case.
guidedQuestion.explanation: A constructive speech sets terms and introduces major arguments.

practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A major line of argument
practiceQuestions.hint: Contentions are case pillars.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A contention is a main argument supporting the case.

practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To clarify the debate
practiceQuestions.hint: Definitions set boundaries.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Clear definitions prevent confusion and focus the round.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many contentions are usually easier for beginners?
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Two or three
practiceQuestions.hint: Enough depth, not overload.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Two or three contentions are manageable and distinct.

masteryCheck.prompt: If the judge cannot tell what your plan means, what did you likely miss?
masteryCheck.explanation: Definitions clarify the case and prevent confusion.

name: Evidence Evaluation
description: Judge whether evidence actually supports the claim being made.

lesson.title: Judge the evidence
lesson.summary: Decide how much a piece of evidence really proves, and compare competing evidence.

content.objective: Evaluate whether evidence genuinely supports an argument, and explain why one piece of evidence deserves more weight than another.
content.explanation: Evidence only helps an argument when it actually supports the specific claim being made. To judge a piece of evidence, ask four things. FIT: does it address this exact claim, or something merely nearby? SOURCE: who produced it, is their expertise relevant, and are there incentives that call for extra scrutiny? METHOD: how was the conclusion reached — who was studied, was there a real comparison, could something else explain the result? INTERPRETATION: does the conclusion claimed actually follow, or is the speaker stretching the evidence past what it shows? When two pieces of evidence conflict, compare them on these same questions instead of picking the one you like.
content.whyMatters: Rounds are full of confident citations. The debater who can say WHY one piece of evidence deserves more weight — not just that a source exists — gives the judge a reason to prefer their side, and spots the moment an opponent's conclusion goes further than their evidence.
steps: Check fit: restate the exact claim and ask whether the evidence is about that claim.
Check source and method: relevant expertise, reasons for caution, who was studied, and whether anything else could explain the result.
Check the conclusion: say plainly what the evidence does prove, and challenge whatever is claimed beyond that.

workedExample.prompt: Claim: removing library late fees gets more books returned on time. Two pieces of (hypothetical) evidence: A - a survey where members say they would return books on time without fees; B - return rates tracked at two similar libraries, where only the one that removed fees improved.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Evidence A is more recent, so it is better.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Evidence B deserves more weight. It measures actual returns rather than what people say they would do, and the unchanged library gives a comparison that points at the fee change itself. A is about intentions, which often differ from behaviour — it fits the topic, but B fits the claim.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer compares the two pieces on fit and method — measured behaviour with a comparison versus stated intentions — instead of using a shortcut like recency.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Claim: the new crosswalk made the street safer. Evidence: accidents fell in the month after it was installed. What is the biggest weakness?
choices: One month with no comparison cannot show the crosswalk caused the drop
The evidence is about the wrong street
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: One month with no comparison cannot show the crosswalk caused the drop
guidedQuestion.hint: Think about what else could explain one short window.
guidedQuestion.explanation: A short window with no comparison leaves the drop open to chance and season. The evidence is relevant, but it cannot yet carry the causal claim.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Claim: the gym renovation improved student fitness. Evidence: a survey shows students like the new gym. What is the problem?
choices: The evidence measures enjoyment, not fitness, so it does not fit the claim
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The evidence measures enjoyment, not fitness, so it does not fit the claim
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare what was measured with what is claimed.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Credible evidence can still fail to support the specific claim. Liking the gym is real information — about enjoyment, not fitness.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Neighbourhoods with more streetlights have less litter. A speaker concludes streetlights prevent litter. What should a careful debater say?
choices: Something else, like overall upkeep, could produce both — this needs a comparison before the causal claim stands
Streetlights are too expensive to matter
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Something else, like overall upkeep, could produce both — this needs a comparison before the causal claim stands
practiceQuestions.hint: Two things appearing together is not yet cause.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The association is real evidence, but well-kept neighbourhoods may get both lights and less litter. Without a comparison that separates the factors, the causal conclusion overreaches.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two reports on a teen curfew disagree. One, from a group campaigning for curfews, highlights a single town that improved. The other, an independent review of many towns with its method disclosed, found mixed results. Which deserves more weight and why?
choices: The independent review — it covers the whole pattern and shows its method, while the campaign report highlights one favourable case
The campaign report, because it is more confident
The campaign report, because one clear example beats many mixed ones
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The independent review — it covers the whole pattern and shows its method, while the campaign report highlights one favourable case
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare breadth, method and incentives — do not just pick a side.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Disagreement is where evaluation starts. An incentive to persuade plus a single selected example warrants caution; breadth and a disclosed method warrant more confidence. That is comparison, not source-bashing.

masteryCheck.prompt: Claim: a reading app doubled students' reading skill. Evidence: the app company surveyed volunteer users, who reported big improvement. What is the strongest evaluation?
choices: Self-selected users self-reporting, gathered by the seller, cannot support a claim as strong as 'doubled' — the conclusion outruns the evidence
The evidence is fine because the company knows its own app best
Reading skill cannot be measured, so the claim is meaningless
The study is acceptable because many users responded
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Self-selected users self-reporting, gathered by the seller, cannot support a claim as strong as 'doubled' — the conclusion outruns the evidence
masteryCheck.hint: Stack the problems: who gathered it, who answered, what was measured, what is claimed.
masteryCheck.explanation: Each issue alone calls for caution; together — seller incentive, volunteers, self-report, and a precise 'doubled' claim — the evidence cannot carry the conclusion. Naming that gap is exactly the skill.

name: Parliamentary Debate Roles
description: Understand what each side and speech is trying to do.

lesson.title: Know your parliamentary role
lesson.summary: Learn the jobs of government and opposition speakers.

content.objective: Match your speech choices to your role in parliamentary debate.
content.explanation: Government builds and defends a case. Opposition tests the case, offers counter-pressure, and explains why the proposal should not stand.
content.whyMatters: Knowing the role prevents scattered speeches and helps teams coordinate.
steps: Government defines and builds the case.
Opposition answers the case and creates clash.
Later speeches extend, refute, and weigh.

workedExample.prompt: Opposition hears a vague government case.
workedExample.weakAnswer: We have our own unrelated topic.
workedExample.strongAnswer: We challenge the definition because it is too broad, then argue the plan does not solve the stated problem.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer performs the opposition role by testing the case.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What is the government's first job?
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Build a clear case
guidedQuestion.hint: Government starts the proposal.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Government must define and defend the case.

practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Test and answer the case
practiceQuestions.hint: Opposition creates pressure.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Opposition should explain why the government case fails or is not best.

practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: They guide speech strategy
practiceQuestions.hint: Roles tell each speaker what to do.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Role awareness keeps the team coordinated.

practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Government
practiceQuestions.hint: The case-setting side defines terms.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Government should clarify the terms of its case.

masteryCheck.prompt: If you are opposition, what should you do with a weak definition?
choices: Challenge how it shapes the debate
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Challenge how it shapes the debate
masteryCheck.explanation: Opposition can pressure definitions that make the debate unclear or unfair.

name: Rebuttal Speeches
description: Collapse to the arguments that decide the round.

lesson.title: Win the rebuttal
lesson.summary: Learn how rebuttals should answer, extend, and weigh.

content.objective: Use rebuttal time to resolve the round, not restart it.
content.explanation: A rebuttal speech should answer the most important opposing arguments, extend your best offense, and explain the voters.
content.whyMatters: Rebuttals are where judges often decide the round. A focused rebuttal is stronger than a rushed list.
steps: Pick the key issues.
Answer the opponent's best argument.
Extend your best argument.
Weigh and name voters.

workedExample.prompt: Final rebuttal after many arguments.
workedExample.weakAnswer: I will answer everything quickly.
workedExample.strongAnswer: This round comes down to feasibility versus preparedness. We win feasibility because the plan uses advisory time, and we win preparedness because the impact is immediate and long term.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer collapses to the central comparison.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What should a rebuttal prioritize?
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Key issues and weighing
guidedQuestion.hint: Final speeches decide the ballot.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Rebuttals should focus on the arguments most likely to decide the round.

practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Focusing on fewer winning issues
practiceQuestions.hint: Collapse means narrow the debate.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Collapsing helps the judge see the decisive issues.

choices: A reason the judge should decide for you
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A reason the judge should decide for you
practiceQuestions.hint: Voters decide ballots.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A voter tells the judge why your side should win.

practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: New arguments
practiceQuestions.hint: Late new material is usually unfair and confusing.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rebuttals should resolve existing arguments rather than introduce fresh case offense.

masteryCheck.prompt: A final speech introduces a brand-new contention. What is the problem?
choices: It is a new argument in rebuttal
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: It is a new argument in rebuttal
masteryCheck.explanation: Rebuttal speeches should not surprise opponents with new major arguments.

name: Refutation
description: Use a repeatable pattern to answer opposing arguments.

lesson.title: Answer with refutation
lesson.summary: Use they say, but, because, therefore to build strong rebuttal answers.

content.objective: Write a direct refutation using a clear four-part structure.
content.explanation: Refutation is the skill of answering the other side. A simple structure is: they say, but, because, therefore.
content.whyMatters: This keeps rebuttals from becoming scattered. It also makes your answer easy for the judge to evaluate.
steps: They say: identify the argument.
But: state your answer.
Because: explain why.
Therefore: tell the judge what to do with it.

workedExample.prompt: They say AI literacy wastes class time.
workedExample.weakAnswer: No it does not.
workedExample.strongAnswer: They say AI literacy wastes class time, but it can fit inside existing advisory lessons because schools already use that time for digital citizenship. Therefore, the time-cost argument is smaller than our preparedness benefit.

guidedQuestion.hint: The word because usually introduces the warrant.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The because part gives the reasoning behind the refutation.

choices: Tells the judge the result of the answer
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Tells the judge the result of the answer

practiceQuestions.explanation: Therefore explains how the judge should treat the argument after your answer.
